title: HTTP through an attacker's eyes
summary: Everything in a request is chosen by the sender. See a request the way an attacker does, craft one with curl, and fix a checkout that trusted the client's price.

steps.title: Every byte is the sender's choice
body: Your front-end is one way to talk to your API. It is not the only way. Anyone can send any request, byte by byte:
```text
POST /api/cart/checkout?coupon=WELCOME HTTP/1.1     <- method, path, query: typed by the sender
Host: shop.example                                  <- headers: all of them, even these:
Cookie: sid=9f2c...                                 <-   a cookie the sender may have stolen
X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.1                           <-   'I am an internal address' (is it?)
Content-Type: application/json
{"items":[{"sku":"LAMP-01","qty":1,"price":0.01}]}   <- body: any JSON, any fields

A **trust boundary** is a line where data crosses from someone you do not control to code you do. The HTTP request crosses one. On your side of it, the only things you can trust are what **you** computed or stored: the price in your database, the user id in your server-side session, the signature you verified.
Hidden form fields, disabled buttons, JavaScript validation and a mobile app's checks are conveniences for honest users. They are not security: an attacker skips them with `curl`.

steps.prompt: Can an attacker choose this value, or does your server decide it?
items: A `price` in a hidden form field
The `X-Forwarded-For` header (no proxy of yours in front)
A button that is `disabled` in the HTML
The `role` field in a JSON body
The price read from your products table
The user id stored in your server-side session
The claims of a JWT whose signature you verified with your key
The order total you computed on the server
steps.explain: A verified JWT is trustworthy because **you** checked the signature with a key the sender does not have. An unverified one is just more attacker input.

steps.title: Craft requests with curl
body: `curl` is how you send exactly the request you mean, and see exactly what comes back.
```bash
curl -i https://shop.example/api/products/7                # -i: status line and headers too
curl -v https://shop.example/                              # -v: your request as well (> lines)
curl -i -X PUT https://shop.example/api/me \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-b 'sid=9f2c...' \                                     # send a cookie
-d '{"displayName":"Ada","isAdmin":true}'
curl -c jar -d 'username=ada&password=...' https://shop.example/login   # -c: save cookies
curl -b jar https://shop.example/api/orders                # -b: send them back
curl -G https://shop.example/search --data-urlencode "q=' OR 1=1--"   # encode a payload for you

In the browser, **DevTools → Network → right-click a request → Copy → Copy as cURL** gives you the request the page sent, cookies and all. Paste it, change one field, send it again: that is most of manual web testing.

steps.prompt: The admin page hides the **Delete** button from normal users, and the JavaScript also refuses to call `DELETE /api/products/{id}` unless `user.isAdmin` is true. What stops a normal user deleting product 7?
options: Nothing yet: only an authorization check on the server, in the DELETE endpoint, stops it
The hidden button: without it there is no way to send the request
The JavaScript check, as long as the code is minified
CORS, because the request comes from the browser
steps.explain: `curl -X DELETE -b 'sid=...' https://shop.example/api/products/7` needs no button and no JavaScript. Every rule that matters runs on the server.

steps.prompt: Send your profile back with an extra field, using the session saved in `jar`, and show the response headers.
steps.explain: `-i` prints the status and headers. `-b jar` sends the cookies that an earlier `-c jar` saved.

steps.title: What the server does with it
body: Here is a real class of bug, reported to shops every week. The request:
```text
POST /checkout HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
{"items":[{"sku":"LAMP-01","qty":1,"price":0.01}]}
And what the server does with it:
```csharp fragment
foreach (var line in cart.Items)
total += line.Price * line.Qty;     // the client's price, the client's quantity
return Results.Ok(new { total });       // { "total": 0.01 }: a 49 EUR lamp for one cent
Two inputs are wrong here. The **price** must come from the catalogue, never from the request. The **quantity** must be checked: `qty: -3` makes a negative total, a refund the shop pays out.
Insecure design (A06:2025) covers flaws like this one: the code does exactly what it says, and what it says is unsafe. No scanner finds it; a reviewer who asks "who chose this value?" does.

steps.prompt: A tampered cart goes through the buggy total and the fixed one. What does this print?
code: var lines = new[] { (Sku: "LAMP-01", Qty: 1, Price: 0.01m), (Sku: "BULB-04", Qty: -2, Price: 12.00m) };
steps.explain: The client's prices give a negative total. Catalogue prices fix the lamp but not the quantity: -2 bulbs still take 24 EUR off. Both inputs need a server-side rule.

steps.title: Fix the checkout
prompt: This checkout trusts the client. Fix `POST /checkout` so that:
- each line is priced from `catalog`, whatever `price` the client sends (the field stays in the record: old apps still send it);
The answer stays `{ "total": 49.00 }`. **Run checks** starts the server and sends real requests, tampered ones included.
starter: record CartLine(string Sku, int Qty, decimal Price);
solution: if (cart.Items is null || cart.Items.Count == 0) return Results.BadRequest(new { error = "The cart is empty." });
if (!catalog.TryGetValue(line.Sku ?? "", out var price)) return Results.BadRequest(new { error = "Unknown product." });
if (line.Qty is < 1 or > 100) return Results.BadRequest(new { error = "Quantity must be 1 to 100." });
total += price * line.Qty;   // our price, never the client's
record CartLine(string Sku, int Qty, decimal Price);
hints: Look the price up: `catalog.TryGetValue(line.Sku, out var price)`. If it is not there, return `Results.BadRequest(...)`.
Check the quantity before you add it: `if (line.Qty is < 1 or > 100) return Results.BadRequest(...);`
template: public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
await Dojo.TryAsync("The checkout could be called", async () =>
var r = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/checkout", new { items = new[] { new { sku = "LAMP-01", qty = 1, price = 0.01 } } });
DojoWeb.Status("a lamp 'priced' at 0.01 by the client is accepted", 200, r);
Dojo.Eq("...but costs the catalogue price, 49.00", 49.00m, decimal.Parse(DojoWeb.Prop(await DojoWeb.Json(r), "total") ?? "0"));
r = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/checkout", new { items = new[] { new { sku = "LAMP-01", qty = 2, price = 49.00 }, new { sku = "BULB-04", qty = 1, price = 12.00 } } });
Dojo.Eq("two lamps and a bulb pack cost 110.00", 110.00m, decimal.Parse(DojoWeb.Prop(await DojoWeb.Json(r), "total") ?? "0"));
DojoWeb.Status("a negative quantity gets 400", 400, await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/checkout", new { items = new[] { new { sku = "BULB-04", qty = -2, price = 12.00 } } }));
DojoWeb.Status("a quantity of 0 gets 400", 400, await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/checkout", new { items = new[] { new { sku = "BULB-04", qty = 0, price = 12.00 } } }));
DojoWeb.Status("a quantity of 1000 gets 400", 400, await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/checkout", new { items = new[] { new { sku = "BULB-04", qty = 1000, price = 12.00 } } }));
DojoWeb.Status("an unknown sku gets 400", 400, await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/checkout", new { items = new[] { new { sku = "FREE-STUFF", qty = 1, price = 0 } } }));
DojoWeb.Status("an empty cart gets 400", 400, await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/checkout", new { items = Array.Empty<object>() }));
